Question: Can agents observe their own execution and flag inefficiencies: repeated exceptions, unnecessary gates, redundant steps, slow integrations? Are improvement proposals generated and routed to process owners?
Response: Yes. The Fleet Manager agent analyses completed workflow telemetry to detect friction. Pattern detection: (1) Repeated exceptions at the same phase across workflows (e.g. works council notification causing 3-day delays in German hires). (2) Unnecessary gates — HITL approvals where the operator always approves without modification (suggests the threshold is too conservative). (3) Redundant steps — phases that produce no meaningful state change. (4) Slow integrations — MCP tool calls with consistently high latency flagged for optimisation. The Fleet Manager composes improvement proposals with supporting evidence (metrics, affected workflow count, estimated impact) and surfaces them on the Control Plane for operator approval. Approved improvements feed into the skill crystallisation pipeline — process changes are version-controlled, reviewed, and promoted through standard lifecycle gates. This creates a continuous improvement loop: execute -> observe -> propose -> approve -> update -> execute.
Key Technologies: Fleet Manager agent (friction analysis), OTEL telemetry, Control Plane (proposal review), skill crystallisation pipeline
POC Demo: POC2: After 10 completed workflows, Fleet Manager detects works council delay pattern and proposes proactive notification step. Operator approves update.

Question: Can the platform run variant processes across agent cohorts (different prompts, tools, orchestration patterns) with statistical comparison of outcomes?
Response: Yes. The architecture supports A/B testing through API Center versioning and APIM routing. Approach: (1) Register two skill versions in API Center (variant A and variant B). (2) Configure APIM to route a percentage of workflows to each variant (e.g. 50/50 split based on workflow ID hash). (3) Both variants run in production, producing OTEL telemetry and Foundry Evaluator scores. (4) The Fleet Manager compares outcomes across variants: quality scores, completion time, cost, human override rates. (5) Statistical comparison is produced and surfaced on the Control Plane. (6) Operator decides which variant to promote to 100%. This requires custom routing logic in APIM and Fleet Manager comparison skills — achievable but not a pre-built A/B testing product.
Key Technologies: API Center (variant versioning), APIM (traffic splitting), Foundry Evaluators (quality comparison), Fleet Manager (statistical analysis)

Question: At thousands of simultaneous maturing workflows, how does the platform manage the crystallisation pipeline at scale with dependency tracking?
Response: At scale, the crystallisation pipeline is managed through Azure API Center with dependency tracking. Skills declare their dependencies (which MCP tools they use, which other skills they build upon). API Center maintains the dependency graph. Crystallisation at scale: (1) The Fleet Manager monitors maturity signals across all workflows — consistency of outcomes, override rates, exception frequencies. (2) Crystallisation candidates are prioritised by impact: high-frequency skills with consistent outcomes crystallise first. (3) API Center lifecycle gates prevent promoting a skill that has unresolved dependencies on non-crystallised components. (4) The CI/CD pipeline runs regression tests against the full dependency graph before promotion. Deprecation tracking: when a crystallised skill is updated, API Center identifies all dependent skills and workflows that may be affected. The Control Plane surfaces dependency impact analysis for operator review.
Key Technologies: Azure API Center (dependency graph), Fleet Manager (maturity analysis), CI/CD (regression testing), Control Plane (impact analysis)

Question: When processes change, how are affected agents identified, updated, or retired? Describe dependency tracking across process definitions, tools, and models.
Response: Dependency tracking is managed through Azure API Center and APIM. (1) Skills in API Center declare dependencies: which MCP tools, which models, which other skills they depend on. (2) MCP servers in APIM track which skills/agents consume them. (3) Model deployments in Foundry track which agents use which model versions. When a process changes: (1) Updated skill is registered as a new version in API Center. (2) API Center identifies all downstream skills and workflows that depend on the changed component. (3) Impact analysis is surfaced on the Control Plane — which workflows will be affected, what testing is needed. (4) The deprecated skill version enters 'Deprecated' lifecycle stage — existing running workflows complete on the old version, new workflows use the updated version. (5) Agent 365 supports lifecycle actions (activate, block, delete) for agents that are no longer needed. The Fleet Manager monitors deprecated skills still in active use and alerts operators to complete migration.
Key Technologies: Azure API Center (dependency tracking, lifecycle), APIM (consumer tracking), Agent 365 (retirement), Fleet Manager (migration monitoring)
